questions.title: Can a defendant challenge the voluntariness of consent given by a third party with common authority?
questions.question_body: I'm reading United States v. Coleman and I'm confused about the defendant's ability to challenge Lisa's consent. The court cites Matlock for the proposition that a third party with common authority can consent to a search. But if Lisa had authority to consent because she also lived there, why can Coleman challenge the validity of her consent? If she had legitimate privacy interests in the home, isn't her consent binding on him? Or is the rule that third-party consent is only valid if it's voluntary, meaning the defendant can challenge the voluntariness piece even if he can't challenge the authority piece?

questions.title: Does an officer saying 'we need to come inside' render consent involuntary under Bumper v. North Carolina?
questions.question_body: In Coleman, the officer said "I'm sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure [the kids are okay]" and Lisa responded "Okay." The court found this wasn't coercive. But in Bumper v. North Carolina, the Supreme Court held that when officers claim lawful authority to enter, any consent is rendered involuntary. The officer here used the word "need"—doesn't that suggest legal authority rather than requesting permission? What's the line between an officer expressing urgency/concern versus an officer claiming legal authority that would invalidate consent under Bumper?

questions.title: How does an initial refusal to consent affect the validity of later consent?
questions.question_body: In this case, Lisa initially said "I'd prefer you not" when Officer Kizer first asked to enter. Then after more conversation, she consented with "Okay." Does her initial refusal make the later consent suspect, or does it actually strengthen the voluntariness analysis? I'm confused about how courts treat this sequence. If she knew she could refuse the first time, does that show she wasn't coerced the second time? Or does the fact that the officer kept asking after her refusal suggest problematic persistence that could invalidate the later consent?

questions.title: What is the scope of consent when entry is permitted for a welfare check on children?
questions.question_body: Lisa consented to officers entering to check on her children's welfare. Once inside, officers located Coleman, asked the children questions about their parents' fight, and learned about the gun—which led to a search warrant. The court found this was within the scope of consent. But if she only consented to checking on the kids' safety, were the officers allowed to ask the children investigative questions about domestic violence? How does the 'objective reasonableness' standard from Florida v. Jimeno apply here—would a reasonable person understand that consenting to a welfare check includes answering questions about potential crimes witnessed by the children?

questions.title: Why is the voluntariness of consent reviewed for clear error rather than de novo?
questions.question_body: The Coleman court states that it reviews the district court's finding of voluntary consent for clear error. But determining whether consent was voluntary seems like a mixed question of law and fact—applying the 'voluntary' legal standard to the factual circumstances. Aren't Fourth Amendment questions usually reviewed de novo? What makes the voluntariness inquiry different such that it gets deferential clear error review? And what exactly am I supposed to be looking for when the appellate court says the district court 'committed no clear error'?

questions.title: Why did the court decline to address exigent circumstances as an alternative basis for affirmance?
questions.question_body: The government argued in the alternative that exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery would have justified the entry even if Lisa's consent was invalid. The court said these alternative arguments didn't need to be addressed since consent was valid. But what if the appellate court is wrong about consent—does the conviction get reversed? I thought appellate courts often addressed alternative arguments to provide complete reasoning. Is there a doctrine about when courts will or won't address alternative arguments? And does declining to reach exigent circumstances mean the court thinks consent was the stronger theory?
